glance_takeaway: A company (Fernwick) search-platform team is choosing a vector-search engine. Four engines were bench-tested; pgnearest and Braid fail hard must-have requirements (a gate M1-M5 — Braid despite being fastest at 12 ms/0.98 recall, because its filtered recall collapses to 0.71), leaving Quiver (managed SaaS) and Hearth (self-hosted) as survivors with no dominant winner. The recommendation is conditional: Hearth if the approved infra hire and a >=4-engineer on-call rotation are committed by 2026-10-01; otherwise Quiver with a mandatory budgeted exit plan — with cost the deciding factor at scale (Quiver cheapest at 1M vectors but far pricier at 10M-100M; labor-adjusted crossover ~30M/~2029) rather than raw speed.

F1.note: Card 1 'Full detail' lists M1-M5 with exact thresholds: p95 <=100 ms incl. filtered, recall@10 >=0.92, filtered recall >=0.90 down to 5% selectivity, EU residency, <=$2,500/mo at ~10M.

F2.note: Card 1 keyfig: '4.1M vectors today -> ~8M mid-2027 -> ~16M mid-2028 (2x/yr)'; detail adds '100M-vector mark is a 4-5 year horizon' and '30% of queries carry metadata filters... grown every quarter'.

F3.note: Card 2: dates 2026-06-08 to 06-19, one frozen 10M snapshot, identical hardware for self-hosted (Quiver measured via VPC peering, ~2 ms hop included), 48-h log replayed at 120 QPS, recall vs exact brute-force on 10,000 queries.

F4.note: Criteria matrix row 'p95 latency, unfiltered': Quiver 18 ms, Hearth 41 ms, pgnearest 95 ms, Braid 12 ms (bolded fastest).

F5.note: Matrix row 'Recall@10, unfiltered (M2)': 0.97 / 0.94 / 0.89 (only pgnearest marked X) / 0.98 (bold best).

F6.note: Hero fail box 'OUT — fails M1 + M2: p95 filtered 110 ms (limit 100) - recall@10 0.89 (floor 0.92)'; card 3 deep dive repeats both numbers.

F7.note: Hero fail box 'fails M3: filtered recall 0.71 @5% selectivity — structural; fastest raw engine (12 ms p95 - 0.98 recall) — still out'; card 3 detail: 'no native filtered search... post-hoc... 0.71 at 5%... structural, not tunable'.

F8.note: Card 4: both pass all five; Hearth '0.90 at 5% selectivity — exactly at the M3 floor... 0.86 at 1%'; Quiver 'held 0.95 even at 1% selectivity'; hero tradeoff panel repeats it.

F9.note: Matrix row 'Cost @1M': Quiver $180 (bold cheapest), Hearth $520, pgnearest $240, Braid $210.

F10.note: Matrix + cost card: $1,900 vs $1,400 at 10M, $23,000 vs $6,800 (detail says '3.4x') at 100M; pgnearest ~$13,500 (est.) and Braid ~$4,200 (est.+DIY) flagged as estimates for eliminated options.

F11.note: Cost card skim + chart: infra crossover ~3M 'already behind us at today's 4.1M ($740 vs $520)'; labor detail '~0.2 FTE = $2,800/mo loaded... cheaper in total until roughly 30M vectors — around 2029'.

F12.note: Card 4 detail: Quiver 'effectively zero FTE. Vendor on-call, 99.9% SLA'; Hearth '~0.5 FTE for the first quarter... ~0.2 FTE steady-state, plus a >=4-engineer on-call rotation... req PLAT-7... approved but not yet filled'.

F13.note: Card 4: Quiver lock-in 'highest of the four... exit... ~3 engineer-weeks today, growing'; 'In-VPC deployment is not offered — N1 unsatisfiable, ever'; Hearth 'Lock-in: low... in our VPC, EU region'; card 7 ties N1 to 2027 enterprise contracts.

F14.note: Card 7 detail: Hearth IF PLAT-7 signed & started by 2026-10-01 AND >=4-eng on-call in writing; else Quiver with mandatory exit plan — SearchIndex adapter, quarterly export drill into scratch Hearth cluster, standing ~3 eng-week budget, re-evaluate at 30M or first renewal.

F15.note: Hero 'Standing override (S1)' box + card 6 S1 + card 7 caveat: filters >60% of traffic or selectivity commonly <2% -> Quiver regardless of the hire; 'checkpoint 2026-10-01 - full review 2027-01-15' appears in byline, hero, and card 7.

strengths: All 15 ground-truth facts conveyed with correct numbers and directionality; nothing distorted or oversold.

The glance layer genuinely carries all four critical takeaways: the headline states elimination + conditionality, and the five stat tiles are literally the takeaways ('Cost ranking inverts with scale', 'Benchmarks did not decide this').

The hero SVG makes the decision STRUCTURE visible — must-have gate, eliminations distinct from tradeoffs, and an IF/THEN box with the standing override — exactly what the brief says flat feature lists fail at.

Cost chart is honest and precisely plotted (verified log-log coordinates), with the already-passed corpus band, today marker, and both crossovers labeled; estimates for eliminated options are flagged as unvalidated.
Caveats survive: Hearth's M3 zero-margin, PLAT-7 approved-but-unfilled, figures-exclude-labor, Quiver 12-month price lock, pgnearest 'not dead forever' — each in a visible caveat block.
Layered progressive disclosure (headline -> tiles -> skim+keyfig -> collapsible full detail) with sticky anchor nav and expand/collapse-all fits the time-poor tech-lead audience.
weaknesses: Very dense glance layer: the headline is four lines and the fifth tile's big value '12 ms · 0.98' can momentarily read as a positive stat before the label/subtext reframes it as the rejected option.

Key evidence (full criteria matrix, labor math, sensitivity details) lives behind collapsed <details>; a reader who never expands sees only skim summaries, and collapsed state also defeats in-page text search unless 'Expand all' is pressed.
Hero SVG fail-box annotations are ~10.5px — legible on desktop, strained on smaller screens; the SVG relies on horizontal scroll below ~1000px.
Cost curves interpolate straight lines between only three sampled points per series in log-log space; the implied crossover position between samples is a modeling choice presented visually as data.
Some jargon (FTE, selectivity) is defined only inside collapsed detail sections, not at first use in the skim layer.
